title: What It Took to Survive a Night in a Medieval London Tavern (1180)
fullText: In 1180 London, there was a public tavern that ran every night without a lock on the door, not a name on the sign, not a stranger by midnight, not a way out once the curfew bell rang. It served every rank of stranger, merchants, apprentices, soldiers, wool couriers, and it did that nine centuries before anyone said, "Last call." This was medieval England's deadliest [music] room and its own contemporary chronicler was already warning Londoners about it. [music] His name was William Fitz Steven. He was a cler in the household of Thomas Beckett and around the year 1180 [music] he wrote the first detailed description of London ever recorded. In it he named two plagues that killed the city. The only plagues of London are the immodderate drinking of fools and the frequent fires. Two plagues, one burned houses, the other filled graves. Fit Steven wrote it casually as if this was already old news by 1180, which means the tavern had been killing travelers for longer than anyone in London could remember. By the end of the next 24 minutes, you will understand what a real medieval ale house looked like from the inside. You will meet the woman who ran it, the most powerful person in the room, and the reason it was legal. You will taste the drink brewed to trick strangers. You will watch the dice game that killed one man out of three who played it long enough. You will learn the one law that made cheating brewers drink their own fraud in the pillery. And you will learn the single rule that got travelers to sunrise. And you will meet one man walking into that room tonight [music] with 18 days of another man's wages tied against his skin. His name is Hugh, 24 years old, a wool courier out of the Cotsworlds, and the money in his purse is not his. Dusk, London, 1180. The bells for curfew have not rung yet. [music] They will. Hugh is 24 years old, a wool courier out of the Cotsworlds. His job is one that only exists because taverns exist. He walks fleeces from the countryside to London wool merchants and walks their money back. Someone has to sleep in strange rooms every night. He is that someone. Around his neck, under his tunic, a small leather purse tied against the skin. Three shillings, 36 silver pennies, 18 days of a laborer's life, enough coin to buy a horse. None of it is his. He is carrying it from a London merchant back to a Cotsworld cloier. If it disappears tonight, he does not eat for a month, or he loses a hand for it, or both. There is no inn with rooms. There is no lock on any door in London that keeps strangers out. There is no choice. The city gates closed at the curfew bell, and Hugh is inside them. His purse knew the danger before his head did. Somewhere ahead in the lane, an ale stake juts from a doorway. A long wooden pole with a garland of leaves tied at the far end. Fire light glows under the door. The garland means the alew wife has fresh brew tonight. It also means this is where he sleeps. He walks toward it. 36 pennies bumping against his ribs. He pushes the door open. First the smell. Pete smoke from the hearth. Spilled ale soured into the floorboards after months of it. Pottage in an iron pot. Barley, onions, a scrap of bacon fat. Warm human bodies packed close. Then the sound. Dice rattling in a leather cup at a corner bench. A dozen conversations in three accents. The hiss of the cauldron. Someone laughing too loudly. Someone arguing about a debt. The scrape of a bench, then the sight. One long hall, a hearth against the back wall, throwing orange light onto 20 faces, wooden benches lining both sides, barrels stacked at the far end, and behind them, a woman with a wooden pitcher, the alew wife. Every face in the room turns, not to greet him, to price him. The ale steak outside was not decoration. In medieval London, it was licensing law you could see from horseback. A pole meant open. A garland meant fresh brew. Every ale wife in the city was required by the ward to hang one. Prices inside are fixed by ward size. A wooden mug of small ale. A wooden bowl of pottage. A share of a straw mattress until sunrise. One penny. Hugh is carrying 36. He walks to the alew wife, puts down a coin, she hands him a mug, she watches how he holds it, and the woman taking his penny knows more about him already than he knows about this room. The most powerful person in a medieval tavern was a woman. She [music] brewed everything London drank, and the law knew her by name. Brewster [music] is the feminine form of brewer. Every English tax role from the 12th century onward is full of these names. Alice Labsterus, Matilda Labraceresses, Emma the alew wife. Brewing was one of the only trades women dominated. In some London parishes, more than half of registered brewers were women. The reason is domestic. Brewing began as kitchen work, turning grain and water into a drink safer than the well. When it moved from the household to the market, the women went with the trade. By 1180, the alew wife was a small business owner. She bought grain wholesale, molted it herself, brewed it in her own hall, sold it under her own roof, and [snorts] paid tax on every gallon. She was often the lency, the landlord, the cook, the security, and the banker for regulars who kept a running tab against their next wage. She was also the room's intelligence network. Every merchant coming south from the wool towns passed through a room like hers. Every apprentice with a stolen shilling, every soldier back from the coast. She knew which face belonged to which trade, which purse looked heavier than its owner, [music] and which stranger had drunk enough to be relieved of it. She had run this room for 20 years, but her ale came in two strengths, and one of them was a weapon. Medieval London had two ales. Small ale was the water. Weak, [music] thin, 1 or 2% alcohol, brewed daily, and drunk by everyone, [music] men, women, children, over about seven. The average adult drank a gallon a day. It did not get you drunk. It kept you alive [music] because a mug of small ale was safer than a mug from the parish well. The children drank it [music] because the alternative was cholera. Strong ale was different. [music] Strong ale was brewed for feast days, for special orders, for men who wanted to be drunk on purpose. [music] It ran 6%, sometimes eight, as strong as a modern craft beer. The alew wife brewed both. Both went into the same wooden mugs. Both looked the same in the fire light. The regulars knew which was which. [music] The stranger did not. Here is how the trap closed. You order small ale because small ale is what you know. [music] She pours you strong. The mugs are the same wood. The room is the same fire light. Three mugs in. You have consumed 6 days of [music] drinking in a single hour. You cannot count your coins anymore. The ale wife counts them for you. Your purse is lighter when you leave or you do not leave. The ale was the water. The strong ale was the [music] weapon. The trap worked so reliably that one English poet [music] nearly two centuries later would write down the whole script because he watched it happen. His name was William Langland. [music] His poem Pierers Plowman is a 14th century work, but the tavern inside it is older than the poem. Every English city had run this room for 200 years [music] by the time he wrote it down. His character Glutton [music] wakes on a Friday morning and sets out for church to confess. He passes an ale house. The alew wife calls him by name because she knows all her regulars and offers him pepper, spices, fresh brew, a warm hearth. Glutton hesitates. [music] He is on his way to confess his sins, but he has never turned down a drink. 2 days later, Glutton wakes on the ale [music] house floor. His purse is empty. His clothes have been vomited into. [music] He has drunk his entire wage. He has missed both confession and Sunday mass. He is a stock character [music] because his story was on every English street. Meanwhile, at the tavern's corner bench, the dice [music] come out. The game is called Hazard. Two dice. 10 men crouched around a table. Loaded dice from the same period still sit in museum drawers today. Weighted with mercury, drilled and refilled with lead. Some of them survived seven centuries in the [music] dirt of Cheapside. Every medieval coroner's role from London tells the same pattern. [music] Dice game. An argument over a shilling. A knife pulled. a body on the floor [music] before the ward watch reaches the door, but the law had its own table in this room, and its punishments were brewed to be tasted. Medieval England regulated ale before it regulated bread. [music] The asai of ale passed under Henry III in 1266 set the price of a gallon by the price of a bushel of barley. It fixed strength, size, and vessel, and it created an office called the Aecon Connor. The Aecon Connor walked the streets of every English town. His job was to taste every brew in the city. He wore leather breaches. He would enter an ale house, order a mug of the day's brew, pour half of it onto a wooden bench, and then sit in the puddle for 30 minutes without moving. If his breaches stuck to the bench when he stood up, [music] the alew wife had added sugar to boost fermentation. If they did not, her ale was pure. Fraud was punished on a ladder. First offense, a fine. Second offense, the hurdle. The offender dragged through town on a sled tied behind a horse. Third offense, the pillery. head and hands locked in wood at Market Cross while the neighbors threw things at your face. The fourth offense made history. In 1364, a London tavern named John Penrose was caught watering his wine. The court sentenced him to drink the remainder of his own barrel in the pillery before the customers he had cheated. The medieval saying went, "Good ale is meat, drink, and cloth." The law meant it literally. Then the curfew bell rings. The door is barred from the inside and Hugh realizes the most dangerous part of the night hasn't started yet. K refur Norman French for cover the fire. The bell rings from a parish tower. The alew wife banks her hearth. Coals rad to the center. [music] Ash pulled over them. No open flame in London after dark. The city has burned three times in living memory. The door is barred, which means the room is now sealed with everyone inside. The mattress upstairs is straw ticking on a wooden frame, 6 ft by 6. It sleeps four strangers, boots on, [music] shoulderto-shoulder. Waking up robbed is a routine entry in the coroner's roles. There are no locks. [music] There is no watchman inside the room. There is one rule that got travelers to sunrise. [music] You do not put your money down. You do not put your money under the mattress. You do not put your money in your boot. You sleep on your money. Purse against skin. Coins as pillow. Back to the wall. Hand on the knot of the purse cord all night. If you feel it move, you wake and you fight. Hugh climbs the stairs. [music] He lies down on the outside edge of the mattress. His back against the wooden wall, his knees pulled up, [music] his hand on the leather cord under his tunic. The room breathes around him. Someone snores. Someone shifts. A rat [music] somewhere below. He does not sleep. He waits. Dawn comes gray through the shutter. Hugh survived the room, but the room itself never died. The ale stake above the door. Every pub in England still hangs one. [music] A wooden sign jutting horizontally from the wall, visible from the street. The garland became a painted board. The board became a name. But the sign is the same object mounted [music] the same way, doing the same job it did in 1180. [music] The alewife behind the bar, she became the land lady. The word Brewster [music] fell out of English, but the woman running an English pub tonight is a direct descendant of the 12th century Brewster. Same trade, same authority, [music] same working hours, the asai of ale. The licensing plaque on the wall behind every British bar today, the one that names who is legally permitted to sell alcohol on these premises, [music] is the direct descendant of the Asai. The ale connor became the licensing magistrate. [music] The bench test became the certificate, the shared hall, the great room of an English pub. Long benches, a fire against one wall, strangers packed close, strangers pricing strangers. The same room, the same wood, the same fire light. [music] The medieval tavern did not disappear. It just got a name. Nine centuries, same room, same fire, same strangers. You have stood in Hugh's Tavern. [music] You just called it something else. The wooden pole outside has a name now. The woman behind the bar has a name now. The stew has a name now. The bed upstairs is a hotel room across the street now, but it is the same room. And Hugh would recognize it in an hour. Dawn. The curfew bell of the parish rings again. The alew wife unbarss the door. The gates of [music] London open. The lanes flood with carts. Hugh comes down the stairs. He hands his mug back. He pays for the pottage he ate the [music] night before. Small ale for the morning. One more penny. He walks out into Cheapside with the leather purse still tied against his skin. Three shillings in, three shillings out, [music] minus one penny. The price of knowing the rules. He was not lucky. He was educated. He knew that ale came [music] in two strengths. He knew that dice at a table have a weight to them. He knew what the ale stake meant, what the asize was for, why the curfew bell mattered, and how to sleep on a purse. The medieval tavern was not lawless. It was a system with a one night entrance exam. [music] Hugh had taken it before. The difference between Hugh's night and yours is not courage. It is a lock on your door. Next time you walk into a pub, English or otherwise, [music] and you find a wooden sign hanging above the door, a woman behind the bar, a licensing [music] plaque on the wall, and a stranger at the next table pricing you with his eyes. Remember what that room used to be. Remember what it costs to walk out of it with your money still in your purse. If you enjoy history rebuilt from the inside, subscribe to Worlds Before Us and tell me in the comments, could you have kept your coins till dawn? Be honest, because the next room we rebuild may lock you in even tighter.
